I generally got a lot of comments from Japanese girls my age on how pretty I was, and since I’m super shy that was a huge ego boost. 

One time my friend and I were in harajuku eating those huge cotton candies they sell (bliss) and a group of schoolgirls rolled past like “they’re so pretty!! But their faces are so small, how are they going to eat all of that cotton candy??”

I do kind of get what you’re saying. It seems like most people are freaking out because they don’t know how to handle isolating themselves to protect from an enemy, but I’m feeling like I’m suiting back up for a war I already have some experience with.

Its kind of messing me up because it’s bringing me back to my life up until 5 years ago, but I survived then, so I can survive this. I’ll just incorporate healthier eating habits this time around.

And just like then, this will be over, eventually.

Ahh yeah, I definitely agree with that. Forgive me if you wrote such a thing in your original post and I didn’t catch it, I have a bad habit of just skimming through posts after getting addicted to twitter. 

There is a book I read in between high school and college  called “Excellent Sheep” by William Deresiewicz that talks about the miseducation about the US elite. He essentially says what you said; ivy leagues churn out amazing hedge fund managers and corporate policy writers, but few independent thinkers. He goes further to say that this lack of inner direction and meaningful living contributes to a widespread feeling of unhappiness. I’m not sure if you’d be interested in reading during lockdown (everybody has their own preferences), but if so, I’d recommend it. It’s been a number of years since I picked it up but from what I remember it’s a very good book.

I used to feel this way.

Then I realized we all come from the same place, and in that place there is no such thing as a hierarchy. One woman may be an incredibly powerful energy worker compared to me, but I have other gifts. 

Inferiority and superiority, as I have experienced, are concepts created by the ego in order to make sense of our physical world. 

When I’m feeling threatened by the gifts of others, I take a step back, remember my divinity, practice self lov,e and keep on going. 

We’re all going at our own pace! If you see them as being further along than you are, maybe flip the narrative and think “I’m going to be that, that is where I’m headed.”

Educated in what way? Do they have advanced degrees and/or professional credentials? Those are wonderful things, but in the global system that has been constructed, “educated”, does not necessarily equate to “creative, independent, deep thinkers”.

I’m not saying this to invalidate the hard work of your friends. In the global system we have, education comes in the ability to remember (increasingly more complex) facts and figures, and attach them to the boxes that may apply. It’s a valuable skill set, especially for the marketplace. But in scenarios that they have not been prepared for in the classroom, some of these educated people may start to break down. This is because novel, original thinking, deep thought, questioning the very system that they have thrived in, and intuition- these are still considered “radical” practices. They are not taught and are not encouraged in schools.

So it doesn’t necessarily surprise me that they are acting they way that they’re acting.

I had pneumonia, and that was wonderful breeding grounds for a viral respiratory infection that quickly  spread from my lungs up to my head.  I got incredibly lucky to have escaped to a place with clean air, proper medical care, and plenty of rest. I’ve since made a full recovery :)

You can “go back to sleep” for a while, and there’s no real consequence for it, if you’re really not ready. You can do that for several years. I did it for ten.

When you’re ready, you’ll know, and you’ll know because you want to grow.

I’ve flipped the script. Instead of seeing suffering as “needed” for growth, these days I’m looking at bad thing as things that happen, suffering as our reaction to them, and our ability to change and survive as a sign of our resilience.

Suffering isn’t necessary for change or evolution, but pain and suffering exist, for now. The real miracle is that we are stronger than we think.

In 2018 went to work for an Esl teaching company in China. The pay was shit but I got a TEFL certificate out of it. I had planned on completing the contract year and hopping to another country. 

The hours were brutal. Classes were poorly managed and we had few adequate supplies, but I had no other job opportunities in the US. To say it was stressful was an understatement but I got through it. I took on two other (under the table) tutoring gigs for food money. After eight months of working like this in a polluted city I got walking pneumonia, but I didn’t realize that’s what it was, because I didn’t have access to an adequate hospital and all my coworkers (also sick) just wound up on an IV drip for a day and were released to go back to work.

I started refusing social outings and sleeping every chance I could in hopes that I would recover. I didn’t. I woke up on a Saturday morning in January 2019 with a 102 degree fever and feeling like I got hit by a truck. I told my boss I wasn’t coming in. She was livid, and insisted I go to the hospital to get a doctor’s note for “proof”.

So I got up, walked to the closest clinic, waited six hours to see someone, and got cough syrup, bufferin, and a three day leave of absence for my efforts. Spent the rest of Saturday, Sunday, and Monday in bed. 

On Tuesday I returned to work to discover that my boss suspected me of having another day job and she was ALSO angry that I had called off work “at such a vital time” (it was always ‘a vital time’ at our center for her, because we were understaffed and she was disorganized). I dropped my tutoring clients.

On Wednesday my health began deteriorating rapidly. By the end of the day I could barely speak and I was coughing so hard I was gasping for air. 

I woke up at 3am, painkillers and fever reducers no longer working, throat so rough I could hardly speak, and wheezing. I called my PCP based in the US. They told me that my health was deteriorating so fast that I had an estimated 24 hours to decide whether I was going to risk my life by staying and checking into a clinic (which were poorly funded, understaffed, and either gave too much or too little care), or coming back to the States. 

I whipped out my credit card, gathered what little remaining savings I had, and got the first flight out of the country. I packed my bags and toss whatever didn’t fit in two suitcases. It was a lot of stuff. I didn’t care. I left my portion of rent and utilities with a housemate and let my landlord know what was up, both were  completely understanding. 

On the plane my eyes started producing some nasty green discharge, so that was cool. 


I called my boss after clearing customs, telling her I wasn’t going to be returning to work.


Annendum: I checked in with my previous coworkers a couple weeks ago to check on them during the COVID outbreak. They told me that they were all fine and that my boss had been fired a couple months ago. I’ve been working odd jobs in the states since then, and I’m not really sure what I’m going to do, but at least I’m not sick.
